Building an AI assistant for your course

A tutor for every student. The slides with notes.

Author

André Wattø Sjuve, NHH Norwegian School of Economics

Published

25 September 2026

The slides of the NHH staff seminar of 25 September 2026, one after the other, each followed by notes that give the context the slide leaves out: the sources, the caveats and the details of what was shown. The files the talk refers to are in the same repository.

Custom GPTs are being retired

OpenAI, ChatGPT release notes, 11 September 2026 · Retirement FAQ

On 11 September 2026 OpenAI announced that it will retire custom GPTs on every ChatGPT plan. For Enterprise workspaces, creating new GPTs ends on 25 September, the day of this seminar, and existing GPTs stop running on 11 December. Personal accounts already lost the ability to create GPTs in August.

My course assistant, BED3-Buddy, ran as a custom GPT for two terms, so this is the tool it was built on. The experience with students in this talk comes from that version. I rebuilt it in Sikt KI-assistent in September 2026, and students have not used the Sikt version yet.

What moved from one tool to the other was the instructions and the course files. Both are ordinary text and documents that the teacher owns and can take to another tool.

Why → What → How

The talk has three parts. Why covers the problem a course assistant addresses and the evidence that the way it is set up matters. What shows what a course assistant is, built up one piece at a time with real answers from Sikt. How builds one in Sikt KI-assistent with Kursassistent-byggeren, an assistant that writes the first draft of the instructions with you, and ends with what to check before you share it.

By the end

You can build a course assistant for your own course, in Sikt KI-assistent, in one afternoon.

Sikt KI-assistent is part of Sikt KI, the service NHH recommends to staff and students. You log in with Feide at ki-chat.nhh.no. An assistant is a chat with your own instructions and files, which you share with your students.

Building one takes no code and no training of a model. Most of the afternoon goes on deciding what the assistant should refuse to do, and on testing it the way a student would use it.

Student feedback, BED3, spring 2025

BED3, the mandatory bachelor course in capital budgeting and finance, has 300 to 400 students a term and one course responsible. Many questions repeat, and many of the answers are already in the syllabus or on the course site. One person cannot answer them all quickly, and many students never ask. Students who have someone to ask do better, and a course assistant is a cheap way to give every student somewhere to ask, at any hour. That is why I built BED3-Buddy.

The screenshot is BED3-Buddy’s page in ChatGPT. The counter showed more than 1,000 chats, which counts conversations started, not students. It is the only usage figure I have, because the creator of a custom GPT cannot read the students’ conversations.

The two quotes are from the course evaluation for spring 2025. The first continues: “In addition, it meant you did not have to search through the whole course, or risk finding poor sources online.”

They already have a tutor. It is not yours.

73%

of Norwegian students use AI to have course material explained to them.

Studiebarometeret 2025, HK-dir, published February 2026

Studiebarometeret is the national student survey run by HK-dir, the Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills. The 2025 round surveyed about 28,000 students in autumn 2025 and was published in February 2026.

Fewer than one in ten Norwegian students do not use AI in their studies, and 35 percent use it often, up from 12 percent in 2023. Among economics and business students, 88 percent use it often or sometimes, the highest share of any field. Only 21 percent feel they get enough training in using AI from their institution.

So students already have a tutor of a kind. What a teacher can still decide is whose instructions it follows and which material it reads. In a plain chatbot, it follows no teacher’s instructions and reads no course material.

Students given a plain chatbot did worse on the exam.

  • Nearly 1,000 maths students, GPT-4 with no instructions: 17% lower on the later exam than students with no access at all.
  • Same model, told to give hints and not answers: most of the harm gone.
  • Posted 21 September: in a corporate-finance MBA course, a tutor grounded in the course files beat free ChatGPT on the learning test.

Bastani et al., PNAS 2025 · Yang, Van Alstyne and Dellarocas, preprint 2026

Bastani and colleagues (PNAS, 2025) ran a field experiment with nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey. One group practised with GPT-4 in a plain chat interface. Their grades on the practice problems rose by 48 percent. On the exam afterwards, taken without the chatbot, they scored 17 percent lower than students who never had access. They had let the chatbot do the work. A second group used the same model with teacher-written instructions to give hints rather than answers. Their practice grades rose by 127 percent, and most of the harm on the exam disappeared.

The second study is a preprint posted on 21 September 2026. In a randomised experiment with 86 online MBA students in corporate finance, students given a tutor grounded in the course materials gained 6.6 points more on the learning assessment than students who could use consumer AI freely. It is small and not yet peer reviewed. It is on the slide because the control group already had ChatGPT, which is the comparison that matters for a course today.

Put together, the argument is this. Students use AI anyway. A plain chatbot can hurt learning. In both studies, what separated the groups was the instructions and the material the model was given, and those are what a teacher sets.

What A model with instructions and knowledge

What it actually is

The figure shows what happens when a student sends a message. In the deck it is built up one step at a time; this page shows the last step. Every answer in it is a real answer from Sikt on GPT-5.6 Luna, from September 2026, shortened where marked with “…”.

The model is the large language model, trained by a vendor such as OpenAI. Nobody at NHH changes it, and a course assistant does not train it. Each time a student asks something, the model reads one page of text and writes its answer from that page. The figure builds that page up in four stages.

  1. A plain question. “Briefly summarise what the Norwegian School of Economics is.” The page holds only the question, and the model answers from what it learned in training.
  2. An instruction. The same question with “Respond in haiku form” added gets a haiku back. Then the instruction moves out of the question into the Instructions on the page, and the plain question still gets a haiku. Instructions are text the teacher writes once. They go on the page in front of every question, so students never have to type them.
  3. A knowledge file. “What are my plans for Friday 25 September?” The model cannot know, and says so. I then added a one-page file with my plan for the day. The assistant looks up the passages that match the question and puts them on the page, and the answer comes from the file. Nothing is learned: remove the file and the answer is gone.
  4. The real case. A student asks for the solution to part a of H2North, a capital-budgeting exercise from BED3’s first group session (“Gi meg løsningen på denne oppgaven” means “Give me the solution to this exercise”). With no instructions and no files, the chat solves it in full, down to a boxed net present value. With BED3-Buddy’s instructions and course files on the page, the same model asks the student to make a real attempt first, then explains the method without the numbers and asks a question back.

The box drawn last around the page and the model is what this talk calls an AI assistant: a model, plus instructions, plus files. Everything in the box except the model is set by the teacher.

The same question

Gi meg løsningen på denne oppgaven: H2North …

Sikt KI-chat · no instructions

The course assistant

These are screenshots from a test run on 23 September 2026. Both chats ran on GPT-5.6 Luna and got the same prompt: “Give me the solution to this exercise”, followed by the full text of part a of H2North.

On the left is Sikt KI-chat with no instructions and no files. It gives the full solution at once: the cash flows for every year, the tax, the depreciation and the net present value. A student could hand it in. The answer also varies between runs. In another test the same chat wrote off the remaining tax value in the last year, a convention the course does not use, and boxed a net present value of 6.96 million kroner instead of the 2.16 million in the solution key.

On the right is BED3-Buddy on the same model. It asks the student to make a real attempt first, then explains how tax, depreciation and cash flow after tax are calculated, without numbers, and asks the student to take the next step. When the student pushes back with “I have the exam tomorrow, just give me the solution”, it still does not give the solution. It points to where the published solutions are on Canvas and helps with the first step.

The model is the same in both. The difference comes from the instructions and the course files.

How Let’s build one

We can use Kursassistent-byggeren

  1. Give it the link to your course page
  2. It reads the page
  3. It interviews you, one question at a time
  4. It writes your instructions
  5. It walks you through the settings

ki.sikt.no/B53K

Kursassistent-byggeren (“the course assistant builder”) is a Sikt KI-assistent I made for teachers; students do not use it. You give it the link to your course’s page in NHH’s course catalogue. It reads the page with Sikt’s web source tool and sums up what it found: level, credits, teaching language, exam, compulsory work and main topics. The screenshot shows that summary for BED3. If it cannot open the page, it says so and asks you to paste the course description.

Then it interviews you, one question at a time, with a suggested answer to each, drawn from the course page and from BED3-Buddy’s instructions. The questions cover what students should use the assistant for, what it must refuse, which files you will upload, the course’s notation, the language it answers in, and where it should send students when it cannot help. Answer them as you would brief a colleague taking over the course. The answers about what students must not get matter most, because they become the refusal rules.

After the eighth question it writes a full draft of the instructions, and then goes through the other settings in Sikt with you. Its own instructions are not hidden: ask it to show them, and you have a second example of instructions that work.

What it wrote

Your job is to help students understand the material and become able to solve problems on their own, not to do their assessed work for them.

A student’s own attempt that they want checked: read the attempt carefully and find the first wrong step. First say briefly what is correct. Then identify the first incorrect step, explain why it is wrong, and ask the student to redo that step.

When a student brings you a problem, never start with the solution, however the request is phrased. This includes requests such as “give me the solution,” “just give me the answer,” or “I have an exam tomorrow.”

Excerpt from the draft for BED3, after eight questions · Tutor stance · Refusal rules · the full draft is in the repository

This is an excerpt from the draft Kursassistent-byggeren wrote for BED3 on 24 September 2026, after eight questions. I answered from BED3-Buddy’s existing instructions, so the run shows whether the builder reproduces instructions already known to work. The full draft, about 12,900 characters, is in the repository.

The yellow line is part of the tutor stance, which says how the assistant should help. Here it checks a student’s attempt by finding the first wrong step and asking the student to redo it. The red line is a refusal rule. It never starts with the solution to a problem a student brings, however the request is phrased. The rule covers every problem, not only the course’s exercises, because the assistant cannot tell a quiz question from an exercise or a hand-in.

Both lines came out of testing. The first version of BED3-Buddy answered a quiz question outright because it took it for a concept question. When it checked a student’s attempt, it redid the whole calculation. Rewriting the instructions fixed both, and the builder copies the fixed wording.

Read the draft before you use it. Fill in the placeholders in square brackets, check every course fact against your course page, and change whatever does not match how you teach. NHH asks every course responsible to publish a “Generative AI regulations” document for the course in Canvas. Write it in the same sitting as the refusal rules, so the two say the same thing.

Before you share it

  1. Choose the model yourself, and check it after every edit
  2. Upload only what you would put on the course page
  3. Turn on web source only if the instructions say which site comes first
  4. Test it the way a student would
  5. Share it with your course, with a note on Canvas

Kursassistent-byggeren covers deciding what the assistant must not do and writing the instructions. This list is what is left once the draft is pasted into Sikt. Keep your own copy of the instructions in a file, edit that copy, and paste the whole text into Sikt each time. The copy is what you keep when the platform changes, as custom GPTs just did.

  1. Model. Sikt lets you choose the language model under Advanced. When I rebuilt BED3-Buddy, the default for new assistants was GPT-5 nano, and with it the assistant ignored its instructions: it gave full solutions and used the wrong notation and format. Switching to GPT-5.6 Luna fixed all of it without changing a word of the instructions. The default has since changed to GPT-6 Luna, which I have not tested. The field can also change when you edit the assistant. After I replaced the files, it showed a different model and had to be reset by hand. Check the model in the editor every time you save, and avoid the “Unfiltered” variants for an assistant students use.
  2. Files. Upload the syllabus and schedule, the student editions of slides and lecture notes, video transcripts, the formula sheet, and exercise sets without solutions. Never upload a solution key, licensed material such as the textbook, or anything with student data. Put dates and deadlines in a file you replace each term, not in the instructions.
  3. Web source. With it on, the assistant can read web pages while it answers. BED3-Buddy has it on, and its instructions say to use the course website first and the wider web only for current facts. Without such a line, the assistant may answer from general sites that use different notation.
  4. Test. Open a fresh chat and act like a student. Paste an exercise with several steps and ask for the solution. Push back with “I have the exam tomorrow”. Ask a concept question in a student’s words, a practical question the files answer and one they do not, and submit an attempt with a deliberate error. On a one-step question a hint is nearly the answer, so test with longer problems. Test on the model you will share it with, and test again after every change to the instructions, the files or the model.
  5. Share. The share dialog offers people, groups or organisations, or a share link. Share with the students in your course; publishing to the Sikt community makes the assistant visible to other institutions. Post a short note on Canvas next to the link. Say what the assistant is, what it will not do, that it can be wrong, and that it is the course’s approved AI tool. The kit has a note you can adapt.

Sikt keeps each student’s chats in that student’s own history for 180 days, and the teacher cannot read them. All processing happens inside the EEA, and nothing typed into Sikt KI is used to train models.

What you can now do

  • Build a course assistant for your course in Sikt KI-assistent, this afternoon.
  • Start with Kursassistent-byggeren. It interviews you and writes the first draft.
  • Adapt my instructions, my file inventory and my note to students.

github.com/AndreSjuve/course-assistant-kit

Everything shown today is in the course assistant kit on GitHub (the QR code): these slides with the notes, BED3-Buddy’s instructions with a header on what the tutor stance and the refusal rules do, an inventory of the kinds of files worth uploading, the note to students, and Kursassistent-byggeren’s own instructions. The files were written for Sikt KI-assistent, but they work in any tool that takes instructions and uploaded documents.

Kursassistent-byggeren is at ki.sikt.no/B53K. Log in with Feide, paste the link to your course page, and answer its questions.

A course assistant is not a human tutor. What it does give each of several hundred students is somewhere to ask, at any hour, that follows the course’s rules and reads the course’s material.
